records.sourceFile: Assisted or unassisted Nordic Hamstring Exercise - Resistance exercise determinants at a glance.pdf

paper.citation: Alt T, Knicker AJ, Nodler YT, Strüder HK. Assisted or unassisted Nordic Hamstring Exercise? Resistance exercise determinants at a glance. Sports Biomechanics. 2021.
paper.abstract: This secondary analysis compared assisted and unassisted Nordic Hamstring Exercise in 16 male sprinters using kinetic and kinematic measures across three sets of three repetitions. Assisted repetitions met the authors' execution criteria more consistently and varied less between athletes, and three sets of three unassisted repetitions produced clear within-session fatigue.
paper.tldr: In sprinters, rope-assisted Nordic hamstring repetitions gave a more controlled, full-range movement with less variation between athletes, while unassisted repetitions showed clear fatigue within three sets of three. The study measured execution quality and fatigue, not strength gains or injury reduction.
paper.methods: Secondary analysis of a published cohort: after six familiarisation sessions, 16 male sprinters performed assisted and unassisted sessions (in alternating order) of 3 sets of 3 eccentric-only Nordic hamstring repetitions on an IsoMed2000 dynamometer, aiming for a knee extension velocity of about 15 degrees per second. Assisted repetitions were controlled by an examiner through a rope attached to a climbing harness, and 3D motion was captured with two high-speed cameras and Vicon Peak Motus. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested mode and repetition effects, with Bonferroni post hoc tests and Levene's test for between-participant variability.
paper.findings: Mode differed significantly for every parameter (p <= 0.003): compared with unassisted reps, assisted reps had 17 to 21% lower peak moment, 21 to 82% higher impulse, 45 to 93% longer time under tension, 23 to 47% greater range to downward acceleration and 7 to 9 degrees less maximal hip flexion. Between-participant variability was lower for assisted reps on all parameters except angle of peak moment and maximal hip flexion. From repetition 1 to 9, unassisted reps lost 41% of impulse and 29% of time under tension and gained 79% in fractional angular velocity, whereas assisted reps changed by -11% (impulse) and -5% (time under tension), with peak moment falling at repetitions 6 and 9.
paper.limitations: The abstract's phrase 'except for peak moments and maximal hip flexion' refers to which parameters favoured assisted execution, not to significance; Table 1 shows significant mode effects for both, with peak moment favouring unassisted reps and hip flexion rated a draw. The sample was 16 sprinters heterogeneous in training history and level, a minimum knee flexion of 28 degrees remained even when assisted, and the study did not measure strength, fascicle length or injury outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest assisted NHEs for unfamiliar, weaker or early-stage athletes, so they can complete controlled full-range reps, and reserve unassisted full-range work for athletes whose level allows it. Because fatigue appeared within three sets of three, they suggest considering muscular failure, rather than a fixed repetition count, as the set endpoint.
paper.athleteDev: Impulse, time under tension and fractional angular velocity can be used to check repetition quality and within-session fatigue in sprinters, and assisted reps gave more consistent execution across athletes. The study does not show that either mode produces greater strength, sprint performance or fascicle change.
paper.rtp: Only partly relevant to return to sport. Healthy sprinters were tested, and the authors suggest assisted NHEs may suit patients at early rehabilitation stages, but no injured athletes were studied and no return-to-sport criteria or injury outcomes were tested.

records.sourceFile: Association of COL12A1 rs970547 polymorphism with elite athlete status.pdf

paper.citation: Ginevičienė, V.; Urnikytė, A. Association of COL12A1 rs970547 Polymorphism with Elite Athlete Status. Biomedicines. 2022;10:2495.
paper.abstract: A case-control study of the COL12A1 rs970547 polymorphism in 293 Lithuanian elite athletes from running, throwing, jumping and football, compared with 287 non-athlete controls. The T allele and TT genotype were significantly more common in athletes overall, and the C allele was less frequent in sprint/power athletes and footballers than in controls. The authors also report signals of positive selection at this variant in the Lithuanian population.
paper.tldr: In this Lithuanian case-control study, the COL12A1 rs970547 T allele was more common in elite athletes than in controls, most clearly in sprint/power athletes and footballers. The result is a candidate association from one population and does not establish a performance effect.
paper.methods: Genotyping of rs970547 by TaqMan allelic discrimination in 293 elite athletes (66 endurance, 80 sprint/power, 147 footballers) and 287 non-athlete controls, with chi-square and exact tests, odds ratios and sex-adjusted analyses. Positive selection was assessed with XP-EHH and Tajima's D using whole-genome data from 50 Lithuanian individuals.
paper.findings: The T allele and TT genotype were over-represented in the total athlete group compared with controls (C allele 20.0% vs 33.3%, p < 0.05). Sprint/power athletes (C allele 16.9%) and footballers (19.4%) differed from controls, while the endurance group did not reach significance (C allele 25.0%, p = 0.082). Controls departed from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, and the authors report that the derived T allele shows positive selection in the Lithuanian population.
paper.limitations: The sample is small and limited to Caucasian Lithuanians, so results may not generalise to other ancestries or countries. No phenotype, injury or training data were collected, and only one SNP was tested. The control group deviates from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (p = 0.00005). The text gives genotype percentages for male athletes (TT/TC/CC 65.2/29.5/5.4%) that differ from Table 1 (65.6/28.7/5.7%); the table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: This genetic association does not support using rs970547 to identify, select or develop athletes. Coaches and clinicians should not change training, selection or injury screening on the basis of this genotype.
paper.athleteDev: The paper does not show that rs970547 affects athletic performance or development. Its only use for staff is as a research signal about the genetics of elite status in one population, and it should not guide athlete identification or programming.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It reports no injury, rehabilitation or return data, and the variant should not be used to estimate injury risk or recovery for an individual athlete.

records.sourceFile: Autoregulation in resistance training - Addressing the inconsistencies.pdf

paper.citation: Greig, L., Hemingway, B.H.S., Aspe, R.R., Cooper, K., Comfort, P., Swinton, P.A. Autoregulation in Resistance Training: Addressing the Inconsistencies. Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of autoregulation of resistance training, which adjusts training based on measured or perceived performance. The authors propose a conceptual framework built on the fitness-fatigue model that separates training-driven fitness and fatigue from non-training readiness, and apply it to within-session, meta-session and program-level methods.
paper.tldr: Autoregulation is a flexible way to adjust resistance training to day-to-day performance, but its terms have been used inconsistently. The authors offer a framework that separates fitness, fatigue and readiness, so staff can define and apply methods more consistently.
paper.methods: Narrative review that traces the development of autoregulation from the 1940s to current practice, identifies inconsistent terminology, and builds a conceptual framework from the fitness-fatigue model. The authors then map common within-session, meta-session and program-level methods onto that framework using examples from the literature. No systematic search or pooled analysis is reported.
paper.findings: The authors report that a growing evidence base suggests autoregulation may outperform some predetermined loading approaches for strength and lean mass gains. They report that velocity-based training produced greater strength and countermovement jump gains than percentage-based programs in some studies, and that a flexible nonlinear periodization approach showed no significant differences from a matched program in well-trained individuals. The authors conclude that autoregulation is context-specific and should be viewed as an adjunct to existing practice.
paper.limitations: The review reports no new data and does not apply a systematic method to the cited studies. The authors note that measurement error can cause poorly calibrated autoregulation to be less effective than standard practice, and that the evidence for stopping-velocity thresholds is mostly cross-sectional.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners should define terms such as readiness, fatigue and adaptation before selecting an autoregulation method, because the terms have been used interchangeably. Measurement devices should be consistent across sessions and have suitable validity and reliability, and velocity ranges should be wide enough to allow for typical error. The authors present methods such as repetitions in reserve and velocity-based training as adjuncts to existing programming rather than replacements.
paper.athleteDev: The framework separates changes driven by training (fitness and fatigue) from day-to-day non-training changes (readiness), which can help staff decide whether a performance change warrants adjusting load or volume. The authors state that the framework's effectiveness and feasibility in practice still require testing.
paper.rtp: The review focuses on resistance training prescription and does not evaluate return to sport after injury. It mentions autoregulated rehabilitation protocols for the knee, but it reports no outcome data for rehabilitation and cannot guide return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Balancing the load - A narrative review with methological implications of compensatory training strategies for non-starting soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Clemente, F.M., Pillitteri, G., Palucci Vieira, L.H., Rabbani, A., Zmijewski, P., Beato, M. Balancing the load: A narrative review with methodological implications of compensatory training strategies for non-starting soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2024;41(4):173-185.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of external and internal load differences between starting and non-starting soccer players and of studies on compensatory (top-up) training for non-starters. Per-minute running and sprint values were often higher in non-starters, while total values were lower, and the authors conclude that the effects of compensatory training on fitness and injury risk remain uncertain.
paper.tldr: Non-starters play fewer minutes, so their total running is lower, but their per-minute running is often higher. Top-up training is widely used, yet its effects on fitness and injury risk have not been tested experimentally.
paper.methods: Narrative review of soccer studies on starter and non-starter load and fitness, and on compensatory training, drawing on literature searches the authors describe as of 2023 and 2024. The review also presents illustrative session scenarios drawn from practice. No systematic protocol, risk-of-bias appraisal or pooled analysis is reported.
paper.findings: Adjusted for playing time, male youth and senior non-starters often covered higher standardized distances and high-speed running, while absolute totals were generally higher for starters. Perceived exertion and heart rate were generally higher in starters, and studies of physical fitness show mixed or no differences by playing status. In English professional players, post-match top-up sessions averaged about 17 minutes with about 0.4 km of high-speed running, and in a Spanish study of day-after-match top-up training, substitutes recorded 0.49 km (5 to 15 minutes played) to 1.3 km (30 to 45 minutes played) of high-speed running, which the authors judge still short of full-match exposure.
paper.limitations: The review uses no systematic search, quality appraisal or pooled analysis, so its conclusions are interpretive. The authors note that most studies are descriptive, small and drawn from few teams, and that speed thresholds and playing-time standardization differ across studies. The practical scenarios are illustrative examples from the authors' practice rather than tested protocols.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff planning top-up sessions for non-starters should first review the match schedule, the number of available players and the manager's game model, because these shape the dose. Running-based high-intensity interval training and small-sided games can be combined, because small-sided games alone fall short of match high-speed running and sprint distances. Staff should track sessions against match load per minute as well as totals, and use individualized speed thresholds where possible.
paper.athleteDev: The review suggests that non-starters may receive less high-speed running and sprint exposure than starters, which could matter for maintaining match fitness. The authors state that the effect of playing status on physical fitness is unclear, so top-up training should not be assumed to improve fitness.
paper.rtp: The review addresses training load in non-starters and does not study return to play after injury. One illustrative scenario modifies the session for a player in his first match back from a grade 2 hamstring injury, but this is the authors' example, not tested guidance, and the review gives no evidence that compensatory training changes return-to-play timing.

records.sourceFile: Between microcycle variaiblity of external soccer training loads through the evaluation of a contemporary periodization training model CUPs.pdf

paper.citation: Owen A, Weston M, Clancy C. Between-microcycle variability of external soccer training loads through the evaluation of a contemporary periodisation training model 'CUPs'. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2024.
paper.abstract: This observational study examined week-to-week variation in external training load for the same matchday-classified sessions across an eight-week in-season mesocycle in 37 professional soccer players. GPS-measured total distance, high-intensity distance, high-intensity accelerations and percentage of maximum speed varied substantially between microcycles. Within-player variation on the same weekday was smaller, which the authors interpret as a more consistent stimulus under the CUPs model.
paper.tldr: In 37 professional soccer players, the same matchday-labelled training session varied substantially in GPS load from one week to the next, even though the planned content stayed consistent. Within-player variation on the same day was smaller, but the study had no comparison group.
paper.methods: Observational study of GPS-tracked (10 Hz) training sessions from 37 male players at one professional club during microcycles 6 to 13 of the 2022/23 season, with 564 sessions in total. Mixed linear models (lme4) with player as a random effect compared each matchday-classified session (MD-4 to MD-1) with microcycle 6, and results were reported as the lower to upper limits of fixed-effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals.
paper.findings: Between-microcycle differences were large for total distance (lower to upper limits spanning 1244, 1503, 1916 and 2248 m for MD-1 to MD-4) and for high-intensity distance (80, 86, 375 and 197 m for MD-1 to MD-4). High-intensity accelerations spanned 11 to 25 across the four session types, and percentage of maximum speed spanned 10.2 to 15.4 percentage points. Within-player standard deviations were smaller on most measures, and the authors describe MD-1 as the lowest-load day.
paper.limitations: The study had no control group or comparison periodisation model, so it cannot attribute the observed patterns to the CUPs model, although the authors state the model 'can mediate large fluctuations'. The authors acknowledge a small sample from one club, sessions per player were unbalanced (median 14, range 1 to 31), and positional differences and personnel changes, which the authors suggest may explain the variation, were not analysed. The abstract gives a high-intensity distance range of 80 to 197 m, but the results report 375 m for MD-3.
paper.practicalImplications: The same matchday-labelled session can differ substantially in distance and high-intensity load from week to week, so a single week's values should be read with the wider microcycle in mind. The authors suggest setting daily targets for key metrics, such as high-intensity accelerations on MD-4 and more than 90% of maximum speed on MD-3, alongside recovery monitoring.
paper.athleteDev: The study describes how much the same weekday session varied across an in-season mesocycle and proposes daily targets for key external load metrics. It supports using MD-1 as a low-load day before matchday, but it does not show that the targets improve performance.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It measures squad training loads and reports no injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Biomechanical and neuromuscular performance requirements of horizontal deceleration - A review with implications for randome intermittent multi-directional sports.pdf

paper.citation: Harper DJ, McBurnie AJ, Dos'Santos T, Eriksrud O, Evans M, Cohen DD, et al. Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration: A Review with Implications for Random Intermittent Multi-Directional Sports. Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: This review examines the biomechanical and neuromuscular demands of horizontal deceleration in random intermittent multi-directional sports. It highlights high, rapid braking forces and identifies braking force control and braking force attenuation as the key qualities, with eccentric, reactive, concentric and isometric strength, and braking technique, as possible contributors.
paper.tldr: Braking steps produce sharper, higher peak forces than the first steps of a sprint, so the ability to brake and absorb force is a separate quality to train. Eccentric strength, reactive strength and braking technique are the main candidate qualities, though most of the supporting evidence is cross-sectional.
paper.methods: Narrative review. Searches of PubMed, MEDLINE, Google Scholar and reference lists covered records to November 2021. Eligible studies measured deceleration kinetics or kinematics during straight-line acceleration-to-deceleration tasks or severe change-of-direction tasks with 90 degree or greater turns, in physically active participants of any age.
paper.findings: Braking ground reaction forces peak in the first 10-40% of stance and within the first 50 ms, and total ground reaction force exposure can be up to 2.7 times that of the first steps of a maximal acceleration. In professional soccer, players performed 80-104% more high-intensity decelerations than accelerations (cited from one match-play study). Cross-sectional studies report moderate to very large associations between isokinetic eccentric quadriceps strength and deceleration measures, with a weaker association for hamstring eccentric strength, and link rapid eccentric torque and reactive strength to braking performance.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative rather than systematic, and the determinants come mainly from cross-sectional observational studies, so causality cannot be assumed. Most determinant studies used pre-planned deceleration tasks and whole-body outcomes, and the authors say the link to unanticipated match decelerations is untested.
paper.practicalImplications: Test and train deceleration as its own quality, not only as part of acceleration or change of direction. Include eccentric strength work, reactive strength and braking technique in the plan, and monitor braking loads and side-to-side differences. The authors suggest combining local-specificity strength work with coordinative training, which no study in the review tests directly.
paper.athleteDev: Treat deceleration as a performance quality with its own profile covering braking force control, braking force attenuation, eccentric strength and reactive strength. The review notes that normative deceleration data are not yet available, so it cannot supply benchmarks for judging an individual athlete.
paper.rtp: The review does not test return-to-sport criteria. It may suggest which deceleration qualities to rebuild, since the authors link braking ability to tissue tolerance, but it cannot set return-to-sport thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Cannabis containing THC impairs 20-min cycling time trial performance irrespective of the method of inhalation.pdf

paper.citation: Cheung CP, Baker RE, Coates AM, Burr JF. Cannabis containing THC impairs 20-min cycling time trial performance irrespective of the method of inhalation. J Appl Physiol. 2024;136:583-591.
paper.abstract: This crossover study compared exercise responses after smoked THC-predominant cannabis, vaporized THC-predominant cannabis, vaporized CBD-predominant cannabis and a control condition in 14 habitual cannabis users. THC-containing cannabis altered heart rate and ventilation during exercise and reduced mean power in a 20-minute cycling time trial whether smoked or vaporized. CBD-predominant cannabis had little physiological effect and no effect on time-trial performance.
paper.tldr: In habitual cannabis users who were trained athletes, THC-containing cannabis reduced 20-minute cycling time-trial power whether smoked or vaporized, while CBD-predominant cannabis had no measurable effect. The study is small and laboratory-based, so it is best read as evidence that THC can impair sustained hard exercise, not as a dosing guide.
paper.methods: Semirandomized crossover study. Fourteen habitual cannabis users completed a control visit, then three inhalation conditions in randomized order: smoked THC-predominant cannabis (13.6% THC, under 1% CBD, 100 mg), vaporized THC-predominant cannabis, and vaporized CBD-predominant cannabis (14.5% CBD, under 1% THC). Each visit included 10 minutes at 100 W and a 20-minute all-out cycling time trial, with expired gases, heart rate and RPE recorded; participants and researchers were not blinded and there was no placebo.
paper.findings: During submaximal cycling, heart rate rose by 14 beats/min after smoked THC and 18 beats/min after vaporized THC relative to control, and was significantly higher than both control and CBD (all P < 0.02); maximal-exercise heart rate did not differ. Mean 20-minute time-trial power was significantly lower after both THC conditions than after control and CBD (all P < 0.04), which the authors report as reductions of 5.1% when smoked and 7.5% when vaporized, with no difference in RPE or pacing. Vaporized CBD-predominant cannabis did not differ from control in time-trial power or RPE.
paper.limitations: Only 14 habitual users took part. Regulators required the control visit to come first, so conditions were not fully randomized; the authors note the highest time-trial power was in the control visit and argue any learning effect would, if anything, understate the THC effect. Blood cannabinoids, intoxication and hydration were not measured, inhalation technique was self-selected so the dose was not controlled, and there was no placebo or blinding. The findings cover one cycling time trial and do not show effects in non-users or in other sports.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff working with athletes who use cannabis should ask about THC use and timing before hard training or competition, because this study found reduced sustained output after THC even in trained habitual users. The study measured no effect of CBD-predominant cannabis on time-trial power, but with 14 participants and one product it should not be read as proof that CBD is performance-neutral.
paper.athleteDev: THC-containing cannabis reduced mean power in a 20-minute cycling time trial by about 5 to 8 percent, a decrement the authors judge larger than typical within-athlete variability. Staff should not assume THC use is performance-neutral for hard endurance efforts in habitual users. In this study, CBD-predominant inhalation did not change time-trial power or perceived exertion compared with control.
paper.rtp: The study measured healthy, habitual cannabis users in a single laboratory session and does not address injury, concussion or clinical recovery. Its findings cannot be used to clear, time or medicate an athlete returning from injury.

records.sourceFile: Changes in the Load–Velocity Profile Following Power- and Strength-Oriented Resistance-Training Programs.pdf

paper.citation: Pérez-Castilla A, García-Ramos A. Changes in the Load-Velocity Profile Following Power- and Strength-Oriented Resistance-Training Programs. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2020 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: Thirty physically active men were randomly assigned to a power-oriented or a strength-oriented 4-week program of 8 sessions, and their individualized load-velocity profiles for squat and bench press were measured before and after. The authors report that the power group moderately increased velocity across the load spectrum, while the strength group changed little. They conclude that load-velocity profiles can be modified by a 4-week program and tend to be training specific.
paper.tldr: A short power-oriented program shifted the squat load-velocity profile upward in physically active men, while a strength-oriented program did little. Group-by-time interactions were not significant, so the training-specific claim is suggestive rather than settled.
paper.methods: Thirty physically active men (mean age 23 years, about 2.8 years of resistance training) were randomly assigned to two groups of 15 and trained twice weekly for 4 weeks. Velocity at 30, 60 and 90% 1RM was recorded with a linear transducer during an incremental Smith-machine test and modeled by linear regression, and the squat 1RM was estimated from the individual profile.
paper.findings: In the power group, squat velocity rose at all three loads (effect sizes 0.70 to 0.93; +5.3%, +4.6% and +2.7% at 30, 60 and 90% 1RM), while the strength group showed effect sizes of 0.00 to 0.35; the time main effect was significant only at 60% and 90% 1RM for the squat. Bench-press time effects were not significant at any load; the power group's largest change was at 30% 1RM (effect size 0.67, 95% CI -0.05 to 1.39) and the strength group ranged from -0.33 to -0.06. Between-group effect sizes favored the power group (squat 0.54 to 0.63; bench press 0.25 to 0.53), but no group-by-time interaction was significant (squat P at least .07; bench press P at least .12).
paper.limitations: No untrained control group, a single 4-week block, and squat 1RM estimated from a fixed velocity at 1RM of 0.33 m/s, which the authors say may have confounded results. The sample was physically active men rather than trained athletes, and the between-group effect sizes are not backed by significant interactions.
paper.practicalImplications: Re-test the individual load-velocity profile periodically when prescribing loads by velocity, especially after a block of power-oriented or ballistic work, because the profile shifted in the power group. After a strength-focused block the profile changed little, but this was a single 4-week program.
paper.athleteDev: Re-check the individual load-velocity profile during training blocks when prescribing by velocity, because in this study the squat profile shifted after 8 power-oriented sessions. The bench-press shift was small and uncertain, and strength-oriented work changed the profile little.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: the study used physically active men with no injuries and measured no return-to-sport outcome, so it cannot inform return-to-sport loading.

records.sourceFile: Changes of Power Output and Velocity During Successive Sets of the Bench Press with Different Duration of Eccentric Movement.pdf

paper.citation: Wilk M, Krzysztofik M, Drozd M, Zajac A. Changes of Power Output and Velocity During Successive Sets of the Bench Press with Different Duration of Eccentric Movement. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2019 (accepted manuscript).
paper.abstract: Thirty-three strength-trained men performed three sets of one bench-press repetition at 70% 1RM with either a 2-second or a 6-second eccentric tempo, with 5 minutes between sets. Peak and mean power and bar velocity were compared across sets. The authors report that power rose across sets with the 2-second tempo and that peak power rose from set 1 to set 2 with the 6-second tempo, which they interpret as a post-activation potentiation effect.
paper.tldr: Power rose over three bench-press sets at 70% 1RM when the eccentric phase lasted 2 seconds, while with a 6-second eccentric only peak power rose, and only on the second set. Without a control condition, the potentiation explanation remains a hypothesis.
paper.methods: Randomized crossover laboratory study in which 33 men with at least one year of strength training completed sessions with a 2-second or 6-second eccentric tempo, one week apart. Each session had three sets of one repetition at 70% 1RM with 5 minutes of rest, and power and velocity were recorded with a linear position transducer and compared across sets by repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: With the 2-second eccentric tempo, peak power was 671.6 W in set 1, 702.3 W in set 2 and 713.1 W in set 3, and mean power rose from 467.7 to 480.1 to 492.2 W, with each later set reported higher than the earlier ones (P=.03 to .04, d=0.83 to 0.88). With the 6-second tempo, only peak power differed, with set 2 (587.9 W) higher than set 1 (565.7 W) and set 3 (563.1 W), and mean power did not change. The text reports no significant set-to-set difference in mean or peak bar velocity for either tempo.
paper.limitations: No control or non-potentiating condition, a single 5-minute rest, one-repetition sets, and 1RM measured only at the 2-second tempo, as the authors acknowledge; the authors also say they cannot separate potentiation from stretch-shortening effects. The manuscript is internally inconsistent: Table 1 marks set 3 mean velocity as significant while the text says velocities did not differ, and the Discussion quotes peak velocities for the 2-second tempo (0.69, 0.70, 0.68 m/s) that match the 6-second tempo table (Table 1 shows 0.79, 0.82, 0.81). This is the accepted, uncopyedited manuscript.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors recommend checking power in each set when stacking sets, because power changed across sets here. In this study the 2-second eccentric kept power rising across three sets at 70% 1RM, while the 6-second eccentric did not; the authors' conclusion that slow tempo may suit maximal strength and strength endurance was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: For power-focused bench sessions at 70% 1RM, a 2-second eccentric kept power rising across three sets in this study, while a 6-second eccentric did not. Staff should check set-by-set power rather than assume a gain in one set carries into the next.
paper.rtp: Not applicable: the study used healthy, strength-trained men performing single repetitions, with no injury or return-to-sport measures.

records.sourceFile: Circadian rhythm in sportspersons and athletic performance - A mini review.pdf

paper.citation: Pradhan S, Parganiha A, Agashe CD, Pati AK. Circadian rhythm in sportspersons and athletic performance: A mini review. Chronobiol Int. 2024;41(2):137-181.
paper.abstract: This mini review examines how circadian rhythms, chronotype, sleep, body temperature, hormones, light exposure and jet lag relate to peak athletic performance. The authors argue that training should be scheduled around each athlete's chronotype and peak time, while noting that some reports do not support this. The review is aimed at sport managers and policymakers.
paper.tldr: Peak performance in athletes appears to vary with time of day and chronotype, and sleep loss, naps and jet lag also affect it. Treat the evidence as suggestive: the reviewed studies are small and some contradict one another.
paper.methods: A narrative review of studies found by keyword searches of PubMed, Google Scholar and Scopus, covering roughly the last two decades. Original studies are tabulated with sample, method and outcome (Table 1), and reviews are listed with their main issues (Table 2). No inclusion criteria, screening steps or quality appraisal are described.
paper.findings: The review reports that morning-type athletes often perform better in the morning and evening types in the evening, with one swimming study showing chronotype shifted peak performance time but not peak ability. Sleep deprivation is described as impairing reaction time, accuracy, submaximal strength, endurance, cognition and mood, and studies of roughly 30-minute naps after lunch or before training are cited as improving alertness and performance after sleep loss. Several cited studies place anaerobic power and jump performance highest between about 13:00 and 20:00, while the authors also cite studies that found no time-of-day effect.
paper.limitations: The review does not describe how studies were selected or appraised, and it reports some results from very small samples (for example 6 to 12 participants). The authors acknowledge that a few reports are inconsistent with their conclusions, but they do not resolve these disagreements, and several of the studies cited are not sports-specific.
paper.practicalImplications: Ask athletes about chronotype and habitual sleep timing before setting session times, especially for skill-based work. Protect sleep before competition and consider a short nap after sleep loss, but do not assume a single best training time for all athletes or sports.
paper.athleteDev: Chronotype and time-of-day effects may be worth considering when scheduling skill-based and high-intensity sessions. The evidence is mixed, so treat these as hypotheses to check against the athlete's own data rather than fixed training rules.
paper.rtp: The review does not study injured athletes or return-to-sport outcomes, so it cannot guide return-to-sport timing. Its sleep and recovery material may be useful for general recovery planning, but it should not set return-to-play criteria.
